title: The UN CRPD Guidelines on Intersectionality Just Changed the Game for Disability Rights—Here’s What You Need to Know
content:
Big news for women with disabilities and all feminist disabled advocates, allies, and organizations worldwide!

 




During its 35th Session in August 2026, the 

UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UN CRPD)

 officially adopted the historic 

Guidelines on Identifying and Addressing Intersectional Discrimination Against Girls, Adolescents, Women, and Older Women with Disabilities

.

 




This milestone represents a monumental step forward for disability rights. For the first time, States have explicit, actionable guidance to support their obligations at the intersection of gender and disability.

 




 

Read the official CRPD Guidelines here

 




What Are the CRPD Guidelines on Intersectional Discrimination?}













The Guidelines serve as an authoritative framework developed by the UN

 

CRPD Committee to help States better prevent, monitor, and address intersectional discrimination.

 




Throughout years of UN CRPD country review processes, the Committee identified a persistent, critical gap: 

the specific rights of women with disabilities and the complex, intersectional discrimination they experience are rarely understood or adequately addressed by governments.

 




As the UN CRPD celebrates its 20th anniversary, these Guidelines were issued to bridge that gap—ensuring the convention is implemented to benefit

title: How can a “broken” body cross the world?
content:
How can a “broken” body cross the world?

 




(My experience participating in Women Deliver 2026)




By Gianna Agostina Mastrolinardo

 







(SCROLL DOWN FOR ORIGINAL TEXT IN SPANISH)




 

For me, as woman with a disability, participating in the last edition of Women Deliver in Melbourne, Australia wasn’t simply about attending a conference. This was an intense and transformative experience that tested my own limits, and it also meant that me and my body had to navigate structural barriers that restrict the participation of young women with disabilities in global events such as this one. 

 




 

One full day of traveling, three flights, more than 12,000 kilometers of flying. Never having traveled so far, the magnitude of the event, and not speaking English that fluently all could have been reason enough to justify saying no to this opportunity. However, I decided to say yes. Even though I was afraid, I said yes with the conviction that we must occupy those spaces, because our presence transforms them. 

 




 




My desire to cross the world and be part of what was happening in Naarm was not enough for me to stop thinking of it as something impossible. Support and collective effort were crucial to stripping that last word of the prefix that imprisons dreams. author: Tam Saavedra
title: Conectivas: First Time in (Por primera vez en) CADF
content:
A table of our own: Conectivas First Time in CADF.    

 




 




For many years, we have seen organizations that serve people with disabilities occupy spaces like the Central American Donors Forum (CADF); this year, thanks to WEI’s support, we were able to attend in person, make our voices heard, and become visible in places where we are usually invisible.   

 




We were not there to hear people speak about us; we went there to speak ourselves, for the first time and in first person – as an organization led by women with disabilities.   

 




What did we achieve?

  

 







We facilitated a networking table on women and disability.  

 










We offered support to WEI’s lighting talk on women with disabilities fighting back anti rights movements.   

 










We networked with different actors about how we see – from a human rights perspective- the backlashes in rights we are seeing globally and how we want to be included in the resistance.  

 







They still see us as something apart.

  

 




Most of the donors we engaged in conversations agreed that the disability movement needs funding but struggled to see how to include us into what they are already doing. 

Disability intersects with democracy, protection and gender equality. 

Yes, we need specific resources and at the same time, inclusion is necessary in the actions already put in place.
